title: DeepSeek Harness and Cordis, Explained
description: A technical look at DeepSeek Harness, Cordis, its plugin architecture, traceable sessions and runtime modes, plus what builders should examine before calling it the future of agents.
coverAlt: DeepSeek Harness and Cordis cover: an AI model coordinates modular tools, memory and an execution harness.
lede: The most interesting part of DeepSeek Harness is not that it gives a model more buttons. It is that DeepSeek treats the machinery around the model as software you can inspect and change.

sources.title: Cordis paper: A Programming Paradigm for Spatiotemporal Composability

sections.title: An agent is a system, not a model with a fancy name
paragraphs: When people say 'this model is a great agent', they often compress several components into one label. The model proposes the next action. A harness provides tools, stores the working state, decides when to call the model again, recovers from errors, and mediates access to files or a browser. The observed capability belongs to that whole arrangement.

DeepSeek puts the distinction in plain language: model plus harness. Cordis is the plugin system at the center of that design. Plugins can provide models, tools, skills, sessions, sandboxes, storage, loops, scheduling and interface components. Services and events let them communicate. That framing is compelling because it makes the agent's behaviour a composition you can investigate instead of a mysterious property you must accept as a bundle.

This does not magically make agents reliable. It makes the boundaries visible enough that developers can ask the right engineering questions. Which plugin owns a permission? Can a task be replayed? What data did a search tool inject? What happens when the model or a plugin fails? Those questions belong in the design, not in an incident report after something goes wrong.

sections.title: Why a plugin kernel is a real design choice
paragraphs: A traditional coding agent can ship as one tightly integrated application. That makes the first experience coherent, but changes to its model provider, execution loop or storage can require changing the core. Cordis takes a different route. A kernel coordinates plugin lifecycle, dependencies, services and events. The agent's abilities live in replaceable pieces mounted into a runtime.

That is a useful separation of concerns. A developer can swap a model provider without rewriting terminal access. A team can constrain which tools are available in a particular environment. Someone building an evaluation harness can select a minimal loop rather than inheriting every convenience feature from a production assistant. This is why 'everything is a plugin' is more than a tidy slogan: it gives the composition a unit of extension and ownership.

There is a cost. Plugin interfaces become an ecosystem API, and an ecosystem creates compatibility work. A version mismatch can be harder to debug than one integrated codebase. Authors must decide which permissions are inherited, which services are trusted, how configuration composes, and whether a plugin can silently alter the agent's behaviour. The test of modularity is not how many plugins exist. It is whether the contracts remain legible as the system grows.

sections.title: The session log may matter more than another tool
paragraphs: DeepSeek describes an append-only session log that records what entered the context: system prompts, model responses, tool calls and results, subagent scheduling and context injection. Its Trajectory view can resume, fork, search and replay from that event stream. For debugging an agent, that is an important idea. A transcript that only shows the visible chat omits much of what shaped the outcome.

Imagine an agent editing a configuration file after searching the repository. The useful debugging question is not simply 'what did it say?' It is what files did it read, what did the search return, what tool output appeared, what instruction was injected later, and which edit followed. If a run can be replayed from the same inputs, a developer can compare a fix instead of guessing at the source of the difference.

Traceability has a boundary: a record is evidence about a run, not a guarantee that every future run is deterministic or safe. Model versions, external services, clocks, network results and plugin state can change. And logs may contain sensitive prompts, paths or outputs. Append-only storage improves inspection while raising real questions about redaction, retention, access controls and user consent.
sections.callout: A full trajectory lets you inspect what the agent did. It still cannot prove that the agent should have been allowed to do it.

sections.title: Minimal mode and Code mode change what you evaluate
paragraphs: The developer preview documents several modes: Standard, Code, Minimal and Creator. Standard exposes the full coding-agent toolset. Code Mode presents tools through an SDK so the model can orchestrate multi-step work in a TypeScript program. Minimal keeps the surface deliberately small with a shell tool and a file editor. Creator mode is for inspecting and composing the runtime.

Minimal mode is a particularly good idea for evaluation. A benchmark can accidentally measure a powerful harness rather than the model behaviour a researcher wants to compare. Remove extra tools, fix the budget and expose only what the test needs, then you can test a narrower claim. Standard mode is closer to how someone might actually use an agent. They answer different questions, and both are worth evaluating.

Code mode is also an interesting direction: rather than ask the model to make a sequence of isolated tool calls, let it write a small program that composes tools into a plan. This can reduce unnecessary round trips for structured tasks. It also means code execution is part of the trust boundary. The sandbox and permissions matter as much as the convenience of fewer calls.

sections.title: What should you test before adopting it?
paragraphs: The project remains in developer preview, so judge it as infrastructure under active development. The published project description states that session content is kept locally by default and is not uploaded without consent. But if you configure an external model, a web tool, an MCP service or another plugin, those providers may receive data you send to them. 'Local-first' describes a default boundary, not every path a request could take.

For a real evaluation, try a small set of representative repository tasks in Standard and Minimal modes. Keep the model, task, repository, allowed tools and time budget the same. Compare first-pass completion, tool calls, external service use, retries, patch quality and human review. Record where the trajectory made a surprising choice. A beautiful UI cannot substitute for a clean test.

The idea I like is composability with inspectable runs. The question still open is operational: are the plugin contracts, permission boundaries and state handling good enough for other people to build safely? A preview can show a useful architecture. It takes harder use to show whether that architecture holds up.

title: Gemini 4 Argon Benchmarks: What the Scores Miss
description: Google reports strong Gemini 4 Argon results, but what do the benchmark suites measure, which gains transfer to real work, and what does a different model cost?
coverAlt: Gemini 4 Argon cover: a benchmark arena opens onto real tasks that test quality, cost and latency.
lede: Gemini 4 Argon leads Google's launch charts. The mistake is turning 'leads this test' into 'therefore it is the right model for my work.' The difference sounds small until you see what went into the test.

sources.title: Vals Index v2.1 leaderboard and methodology
Google: Gemini 4 Argon comes to the Gemini app

sections.title: Start with what Google is actually claiming
paragraphs: Google introduced Gemini 4 Argon on September 30, 2026, then announced its Gemini app availability on October 13. The release positions Argon for long-horizon software engineering, legal and finance work, and defensive cybersecurity. Its published examples include a Rust migration, an optimization to a video decoder and an internal memory-use project. These are interesting claims with human and automated audits described as part of the rollout.

Those examples need their labels attached. Google's reported 2.7-times faster libgav1 result compares an Argon-assisted Rust rewrite with an existing Rust port, and Google says output remained identical. That is promising technical work. It is not evidence that any person can hand Argon a codebase and reliably produce the same outcome. Google itself says the large-scale migrations undergo automated and manual review before production.

The launch page reports 77.9% on DeepSWE v1.1, 51.3% on AutomationBench and 91.7% on LVBench. A score is evidence about a task set under an evaluation setup. The three percentages cannot be put on a single scale or added into a claim of general intelligence. Each benchmark measures a different kind of work.

rows: Long-horizon software engineering tasks, as described by Google
That every coding workflow sees a 77.9% success rate
End-to-end task execution across business functions
That a real company's tasks will be completed safely
That the model is accurate across every video or question type

sections.title: The Vals Index is useful, and its design is the argument
paragraphs: Vals AI's October 16 snapshot ranks Argon first at 68.90%, then Claude Sonnet 5.5 at 67.04%. The gap is 1.86 percentage points, which is a lead within this particular index. This is an independent evaluation source, not the same chart Google uses to market the release.

The index combines six private benchmarks and two public ones across finance, coding, legal and tax. It weights the sectors by shares of US gross domestic product, and the site's authors explicitly call that an oversimplification used as a proxy for economic significance. This is a coherent choice if that is the question you want to ask. A student building an Android app, a lawyer doing a cited case search and a tax team do not have the same weighting needs.

Argon cost $15.68 for the index test and Sonnet $21.34 in the snapshot. Those amounts are measured for this benchmark run, not a general per-project cost and not proof of cheaper quality-adjusted production. The table also reports full evaluation durations. Under Vals's configuration, Argon took 46 minutes 33 seconds and Sonnet 5.5 took 1 hour 18 minutes. A difference can matter, but these figures describe a benchmark run, not interactive response latency.

sections.title: An independent security test shows why setup matters
paragraphs: CWE-bench v1 compares agent and harness combinations on held-out audit-and-patch tasks. Its posted table gives Argon with Antigravity a 68% programmatic pass@1 score and a 62% score on the three-judge panel. GPT-6 Astra with Codex scores 68% and 66%, respectively. Grok 4.7 with OpenCode also scores 68% programmatically, then 64% on the judge panel. Those are ties in one dimension and differences in another.

The benchmark explains that its task gives an agent a repository without a named vulnerability, then grades whether a patch blocks the exploit and keeps existing tests passing. Its top results can shift depending on whether you look at the deterministic verifier or the judge panel. This is precisely the point. The judge is part of the evaluation, and 'three models tie at 68%' is more informative than saying one system is the undisputed cybersecurity leader.

The posted Argon rollout costs $6.63 on that test, compared with $2.85 for GPT-6 Astra and $2.75 for Grok 4.7. A buyer may reasonably care about that. Cost per rollout still needs to be read alongside pass rate, task coverage, model pricing date and harness. These results do not prove one system is universally better. They do prove the headline needs context.

sections.title: A benchmark win is a starting hypothesis
paragraphs: If the report shows an improvement on difficult reasoning or coding tasks, ask which tasks moved and which did not. Did Argon get fewer examples wrong, or did it make smaller gains on already easy questions? Was the score measured with a tool-using agent loop? Were the runs repeated? Is the reported difference meaningful under the same evaluation conditions?

Benchmarks can help shortlist a model. For a coding workflow, take issues similar to your own backlog and set up a controlled comparison. Use the same repository snapshot, prompt, tools and stopping rule for each system. Count test failures, unrequested edits, retries and review time. An agent that wins a synthetic coding score but creates more cleanup may be the wrong fit.

The practical conclusion is usually more local than the release headline. Perhaps Argon makes certain multi-file edits easier. Perhaps it reasons well but costs more, or the gains disappear when the task depends on local project knowledge. The benchmark helps form that question; a small repeatable evaluation answers it better.

sections.title: Long-running tasks change the product question
paragraphs: Google says Gemini tasks can continue working across connected apps while a user is away. That changes the failure mode. A chat answer can be wrong and still require the person to act on it. An agentic task can take the wrong action directly unless the product inserts suitable controls.

For a task agent, evaluate success as a sequence, not a single response. Did it interpret the request correctly? Did it choose a safe action? Did the correct account or file change? Could the person see progress and cancel? Did it stop when required information was unavailable? The model's reasoning score does not answer these interface and permission questions.

Progress updates are useful when they make the system more observable. They become noisy when they narrate activity without telling you what the system needs from you. The best product question is not 'can it run unattended?' It is 'what evidence and controls tell me when to let it run unattended?'

sections.title: Keep the claim calibrated
paragraphs: Argon is new, and launch materials will be updated as access and evaluation evolve. A feature appearing in a macOS app does not mean every user, region, plan or workflow has the same experience. Availability, context limits, tools and rate policies can change. Check the dated official documentation before making product decisions around them.

A good first week with a model is not a benchmark. One bad first response is not a benchmark either. Collect a few tasks you care about and make the comparison repeatable. Keep both a quality measure and a cost or delay measure. If the decision is low stakes, a lightweight side-by-side may suffice. If the system can act on data or people, review behaviour more carefully.
Gemini 4 Argon may be a strong model. The release deserves a fair look, not a round of imaginary guarantees. Ask what gets easier for you, measure that task, then make the call.

title: Phonon-2: Open Speech Recognition on Device
description: A close look at Phonon-2's compact weights, reported word error rate, Apple Neural Engine speed, licensing and the real evaluation questions for local transcription.
coverAlt: Phonon-2 cover: a compact on-device speech model turns an audio waveform into transcript tiles.
lede: A speech model that runs locally in seconds is a different kind of release from another leaderboard winner. Phonon-2 makes the hardware and deployment question feel concrete.

sections.title: Small does not have to mean toy
paragraphs: Fermion Research released Phonon-2 in September 2026 as an open English speech recognition model. Its model page lists a 164 MB download, an average 5.21 percent word error rate across seven English test sets on the Open ASR Leaderboard, and 606 times real time on the Neural Engine of an M5 MacBook Air. The same page says models that score better on that seven-set average are at least 5.8 times its size.

The interesting engineering choice is a compact encoder using learned quantization levels, with the team reporting roughly 2.1 bits per stored weight. The project says this lets the small file retain accuracy comparable to its 2.5 GB full-precision teacher on average, while beating the teacher on meeting and parliamentary speech in the evaluated sets.

That is a strong direction: local speech recognition gets practical when a device can run it quickly, privately, and without a GPU tied up by inference. But each number has a scope. The seven sets are English. An average is not a guarantee for one accent, microphone, name or noisy room. The size claim is about download and stored weights, not necessarily peak memory during every runtime.

sections.title: Realtime factor is impressive and easy to misunderstand
paragraphs: A 606-times realtime figure means the system processed audio faster than it was recorded under the stated machine and runtime configuration. Fermion gives the example that an hour of audio becomes text in about six seconds on the Neural Engine. That is a throughput claim for that setup. It does not mean the first word appears six seconds after a person starts speaking, and it does not mean every computer achieves the same speed.

The changelog is useful here because it shows the product work around the model. Core ML runs on Apple's Neural Engine. Other releases describe MLX on Apple silicon, CPU tiers across processor families, CUDA containers, startup speed and timestamp support. The same weights meet different runtimes and hardware paths. That is why users should care about the exact engine rather than quote one peak number as universal.

For live dictation, time-to-first-text and key-up latency matter more than a giant batch's throughput. For transcribing an archive, throughput and memory matter. For a video editor, word timestamps and sentence segments may be the difference between a demo and something usable. Latency is part of the task definition.

sections.title: The 5.21 percent score is one window into quality
paragraphs: Word error rate counts substitutions, insertions and deletions relative to a reference, divided by the number of reference words. It gives a consistent summary of transcript mismatch. It treats errors differently from many users, though. Swapping a filler word might be harmless. Changing 'fifteen' to 'fifty' in a maintenance instruction is not. A misspelled product name can ruin a customer record even if the overall transcript barely changes.

The model page reports a seven-set average. Look up the individual sets and their recording conditions before applying the figure to your own use. Are the speakers conversational, scripted, remote, or amplified? Is the reference text normalized for punctuation and capitalization? Are set sizes balanced equally? The average answers a question chosen by an evaluation, not every deployment question a user might have.

For a fair local check, take permitted recordings representative of your workload, make accurate reference transcripts, and report the overall WER plus categories of errors that would matter. Never feed private audio into an external service without authority. For names and domain vocabulary, evaluate both the default model and a supported hotword setup.

sections.title: Open weights and local inference have real value
paragraphs: Fermion releases Phonon-2 weights under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0. Its model page says that permits commercial use, modification and redistribution with attribution, and notes that the weights inherit that license from the Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 base. The command-line software is described separately as Apache 2.0. Check the current notices before redistributing a product. Open weights, code and license terms are not one undifferentiated thing.

On-device inference can reduce how much sensitive audio leaves a user's machine. That is valuable for meeting notes, personal dictation, or offline environments. 'Local' still does not cover your whole application automatically. A cloud backup, updater, analytics service, crash reporter or external model can receive data through another path. Threat modelling the product matters as much as locating the weights.

The exciting part is that a 164 MB English model can be useful enough to ship in a real dictation workflow. The responsible part is keeping the next sentence specific: useful on which speakers, on which hardware, under which license, for which kinds of audio? That is a far better conversation than pretending a single score settled speech recognition.

title: What AI-Generated Math Proofs Actually Verify
description: How to assess OpenAI's October 2026 mathematics results: what the Lean formalizations establish, what the human-written manuscripts still need, and why discovery is not the same as verification.
coverAlt: AI mathematical proofs cover: a handwritten idea passes through a formal checker to a verified theorem.
lede: A computer-checked proof is the most interesting part of a new AI math result, and also the part people flatten into the wrong claim. Verification can establish a theorem in a formal system. It does not automatically tell you who discovered the idea or whether the surrounding story is correct.

sources.title: OpenAI: Sharing AI progress in mathematics

sections.title: Separate the result from the announcement
paragraphs: OpenAI's October 6, 2026 release shares manuscripts and Lean formalizations for mathematical results proposed with the help of an internal model. On October 15, the company added a follow-up about supporting mathematicians as they assess and build on the work. That is more substantial than a capability teaser because readers can inspect artifacts.

But a company statement is not the same thing as community validation. A manuscript can contain a valuable argument and still need expert review. A formal proof can establish that the encoded proposition follows from the encoded premises in Lean's trusted foundation. That does not prove the formal statement matches every intended claim in the prose, that the human authors identified all assumptions, or that the result is significant in the broader field.

The strongest story is precisely this separation: language models may help propose an argument, while formalization makes one portion of the verification problem explicit and mechanically checkable. The new part is not that mathematics suddenly needs no people. It is that a tool can make some hard checking more tractable.

sections.title: What a Lean proof can and cannot establish
paragraphs: Lean represents definitions, assumptions and theorems in a formal language. Its kernel checks proof terms against those definitions. If the proof type-checks, the formal conclusion follows from the formal premises under the system's foundations. That is a remarkably strong guarantee about the encoded derivation.

The word 'encoded' matters. Formalizing a statement takes choices. Are the definitions equivalent to the informal mathematical objects? Were side conditions preserved? Does the statement say what the paper says it says? The kernel cannot catch a mistaken translation of the human goal into a different proposition. This is why experts still inspect the formulation and the significance of the result.

A good proof repository helps by making assumptions and dependencies visible. Reproduction matters too: can a clean checkout compile the project with stated versions? Are there hidden axioms or shortcuts? A trusted proof assistant greatly narrows one type of error, but it does not dissolve every other kind.

sections.title: Mathematical discovery includes more than getting a proof
paragraphs: A research result involves choosing a worthwhile problem, finding a promising route, deciding what counts as a useful explanation, making definitions, correcting failed ideas and connecting the conclusion to what people already know. Proof formalization addresses an important part of that chain. It does not yet measure every part of it.

People also decide which results merit attention and whether a solution opens a new avenue. A corpus of machine-generated proofs can contain genuine advances and irrelevant formal exercises at the same time. The number of manuscripts is not a measure of mathematical insight. A count is useful for planning review effort, not a substitute for expert assessment.

The most honest and interesting way to read the October release is to follow a claim through artifacts. Which statement is formalized? What assumptions does it use? Who has independently checked it? What changed after the community read it? A verified proof is strong evidence about a derivation. Its place in mathematics is a wider question.

sections.title: What evidence would change the conversation?
paragraphs: Independent mathematicians commenting on specific results, reproducible Lean projects, and papers that explain how verification proceeded would make the story clearer. So would transparent attribution: what the model proposed, which changes a researcher made, where the human found an error, and what was ultimately checked. The development process is itself research data.

For students, there is a useful learning pattern here. Start from a theorem, read the human explanation, then inspect the formal statement and proof. Notice where the informal and formal versions meet. Even if the system did not create the mathematical insight you expected, the artifacts can teach you how a proof is represented and checked.

This deserves curiosity and criticism at the same time. If the result survives expert scrutiny, that will matter more than a dramatic launch line. If it does not, the formalization may still show something useful about how AI systems participate in formal mathematics. Either way, we should argue about the proof people can inspect, not the future we imagine from a headline.

title: Why Word Error Rate Isn't Enough
description: Understand how WER works, which transcript errors matter in practice, and how to build a speech recognition evaluation using your actual microphones, accents and vocabulary.
coverAlt: Word error rate cover: a transcript highlights a costly number and name error beside its waveform.
lede: A speech recognizer can make a small number of word errors and still get the only important number in your instruction wrong. The aggregate score cannot tell you which failure happened.

sections.title: A useful definition with a sharp boundary
paragraphs: Word error rate measures insertions, deletions and substitutions between a reference transcript and a hypothesis. Sum those edits and divide by the number of reference words. It gives speech recognition experiments a common yardstick and is easy to compare across datasets when text normalization is consistent.

But a single edit is a single edit regardless of consequence. A filler word and a changed dosage, account identifier or meeting time can affect the score similarly. Punctuation may not count under one normalization scheme and may matter to a downstream task. WER cannot be used as a complete measure of usefulness without understanding what kind of mistakes are inside it.

Before comparing two systems, inspect how the references were normalized. Are contractions expanded? Are numbers words or digits? Are partial words, disfluencies, case and punctuation ignored? A mismatch in text rules can make an apparent model difference partly an evaluation difference.

sections.title: Score the errors your user notices
paragraphs: Build categories that reflect your task. Proper names, product terminology, quantities, negation, speaker attribution and words that trigger downstream action deserve separate counts. You can preserve aggregate WER and report a critical error rate alongside it. A useful product may tolerate more harmless cleanup if it makes fewer damaging errors.

Audio also changes the result. Compare phone microphones with laptop microphones, overlapping speech with one speaker, close-mic speech with a distant room, clean audio with background noise, and the accents your users actually speak. Do not label a model 'bad on accents' based on a handful of examples. Gather enough examples, describe the group and report uncertainty.

For Phonon-2, the published seven-set average is a helpful reference point for English recognition. A team evaluating it for local meeting transcription should still test meeting recordings, expected vocabulary and available hardware. It is inappropriate to infer multilingual performance from an English score.

Build a names and terminology subset
The decision is assigned to the wrong person

sections.title: Create a small but honest audio set
paragraphs: Start with consented recordings from the actual environment. Write references consistently and record which microphone, language, room and task produced each clip. Include ordinary examples as well as the difficult cases that appear often enough to matter. Never use private recordings simply because they are available on somebody's laptop.

Keep the test set separate from the audio used to tune vocabulary or choose settings. If you repeatedly adjust the system after looking at every result, the score stops being an independent estimate. Keep a development set for improvements and a held-out sample for the final check.
Run each engine with the documented settings. Save the transcript and version. A score you cannot reproduce is not useful when the model updates next month.

sections.title: Quality is only one deployment constraint
paragraphs: For live dictation, measure time from the end of speech to the first useful text and the distribution of delays, not only audio processed per second. For a file archive, measure total throughput and memory. For captioning, measure timestamp quality. These are different user goals and deserve different test metrics.

Local inference can keep audio on a device, which reduces one important exposure route. Verify whether your app sends telemetry, backs up audio, downloads models, or calls a cloud service through another feature. 'On-device model' is not synonymous with 'the entire application never sends data'.

Use a pre-deployment run that includes setup time, cold start, failure recovery, battery use where relevant and the user-visible correction flow. Choose the system that fits the actual task and sensitivity. A leaderboard is a shortlist, not your production sign-off.

title: Compare AI Models on Cost, Latency and Quality
description: A repeatable method for comparing AI models on your own tasks, controlling prompts and tools while tracking success, retries, latency and total operating cost.
coverAlt: Model comparison cover: two matched tests weigh task quality against response time and cost.
lede: If model A gets a larger prompt budget and more retries than model B, the chart does not compare models. It compares two different experiments.

sources.title: HELM: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models
Google SRE Book: Service Level Objectives

sections.title: Freeze what counts as the experiment
paragraphs: Write down the model identifier, date, prompt, system message, tools, temperature or sampling settings, context, retry policy and maximum time. Save the inputs. If one provider's interface silently retries a failed call and the other does not, count that difference instead of hiding it.

Choose tasks from a real workload, not whichever prompt made your favourite model look sharp. Include typical cases, hard cases, and a few cases where the model should abstain or ask for clarification. Define acceptance criteria before looking at the outputs.

For coding agents, freeze the repository commit, environment, test commands and permissions. For retrieval, use the same documents and search budget. For speech, use identical audio and a documented reference. Comparison only becomes meaningful when the conditions match.

sections.title: Measure the work, not just the response
paragraphs: Pick a quality measure tied to user success. Then track latency, cost, retries, human repair time and failure severity. Use per-request values as well as averages. P95 latency matters when a person is waiting; a few dangerous errors matter even when the average accuracy is high.

A reasonable cost per usable result includes calls that are retried or rejected. Count tool calls, search, input and output tokens, preprocessing and review time. When the provider's pricing changes, save the retrieval date and assumptions so the calculation can be updated.

Repeat stochastic tasks. If you cannot afford many runs, be transparent about the small sample and avoid treating a tiny lead as certain. For subjective outputs, blind the reviewer to the model label where possible and make disagreement visible.

Using fluency as a proxy for truth
Success across runs and held-out tasks
Reporting the best of several attempts
Median and upper percentile end-to-end time

sections.title: Write a result someone else could reproduce
paragraphs: Publish the test conditions beside the result. Keep the raw output where privacy rules permit, or provide a safe synthetic test if the input is sensitive. Separate provider claims from your own measurements. A vendor's reported score is useful context, not a measurement you performed.

If the model version is closed or changes over time, label the test date and API configuration. Re-run the evaluation when behaviour changes. Store the test prompts and scoring rubric so future comparisons have a baseline.

The result may be that a smaller, slower or less fashionable model works better for your use. That is a useful result. A comparison should help someone make a decision, not stage a race the test was not designed to settle.

sections.title: Choose with a threshold, not a trophy
paragraphs: Before running the test, set minimum quality, maximum acceptable latency and budget boundaries. Among systems that meet them, choose the one whose operational tradeoffs fit your project. A model that misses a safety threshold should not win because it saves a few milliseconds.

Decide what will trigger another evaluation: a model update, a change to the prompt, a larger corpus, a new user group or an increase in error reports. That makes comparison a living engineering practice instead of a launch-day spreadsheet.
A fair test cannot tell you everything. It can make your uncertainty explicit and prevent a benchmark chart from making the decision for you.
